Split the conjunction and use neighborhood-filter characterizations.

For the first part, interpret  
\(\operatorname{NeBot}(\mathcal N x\sqcap\mathcal N y)\) as saying that \(x\) and \(y\) do not have disjoint neighborhoods. The \(R_1\) axiom gives the dichotomy that two points are either inseparable (have the same neighborhoods) or admit disjoint neighborhoods. The second alternative would make \(\mathcal N x\sqcap\mathcal N y=\bot\), contradicting `NeBot`.

For the equivalence, prove both universally quantified statements independently:

- Put \(P=\{x\mid p(x)\}\). The set of \(y\) such that \(p\) holds eventually in \(\mathcal N y\) is exactly \(\operatorname{interior}(P)\). Thus the left statement reduces to
  \[
  \operatorname{interior}(P)\in\mathcal N[s]a
  \iff P\in\mathcal N[s]a.
  \]
  When \(s\) is open, any relative neighborhood \(U\cap s\subseteq P\) can be chosen open, hence lies in \(\operatorname{interior}(P)\); the reverse implication follows from \(\operatorname{interior}(P)\subseteq P\).

- In an \(R_0\) space, specialization is symmetric: \(x\) specializing to \(y\) forces their neighborhood filters to coincide, and hence \(y\) specializes to \(x\).

Therefore both sides of the displayed `Iff` hold, so the equivalence follows.
